deed: IsraAID sent a team of 14 to Sri Lanka that set up a clinic and kitchens for tsunami survivors
title: IsraAID sent an Israeli team to Sri Lanka that set up kitchens and a clinic for tsunami survivors

trailer.text: After the tsunami of December 26, 2004, IsraAID led the Israeli campaign for the disaster in Southeast Asia.
It sent an Israeli team of medical and logistical personnel to Sri Lanka, with medicines, kitchen supplies and tents.
The team set up a camp with a kitchen run by local cooks, an infirmary and an area for the care of orphaned and lost children.
The campaign was funded by Israelis and by Jewish communities in Europe and America.

glance.label: Funding
glance.value: Israelis and Jewish communities in Europe and America

paragraphs.text: The tsunami struck on December 26, 2004.
According to ISRAEL21c, it left over 250,000 dead, 125,000 injured and almost two million homeless.
Sri Lanka was among the countries affected.
The Sri Lankan government was trying to recover from the loss of more than 30,000 people.
According to Shachar Zahavi, it consists of about 30 organizations and acts as a coordinating center among them.
Shachar Zahavi, the founder of IsraAID, was then a second-year student at Tel Aviv University.
According to ISRAEL21c in 2020, he lived in a moshav in Emek Hefer, a village his Holocaust survivor grandparents helped build.
At the time, Zahavi did not receive a salary, and all the funding came from private donors in Israel and abroad.
Because of the tsunami, Zahavi, 29, stopped studying for a semester in order to work in Sri Lanka.
He said the tsunami had robbed him of the semester.
Israeli doctors were among the first foreign medical personnel to reach Sri Lanka after the tsunami.
Prof. Avi Rivkind of Hadassah said they received a phone call that they were needed, and three hours later they were at the airport.
He flew on Sunday night with three other Hadassah physicians, who specialize in rescue, trauma and pediatrics.
Rivkind said the Sri Lankan government had asked him to visit the hard-hit southern region and assess the needs.
Israel mobilized some 150 army doctors and search and rescue teams, who planned to set up a field hospital in Sri Lanka.
The Sri Lankan government declined the offer, and so Israel reduced the mission.
The plane that left for Sri Lanka on Tuesday night carried 10,000 blankets, 3,680 liters of mineral water, 12 tons of food, 17.5 tons of baby food and more than nine tons of medicine.
The organization Latet also sent equipment, including 250 thousand water-purifying tablets.
According to Sri Lankan sources, this was the largest aid up to then from any civilian organization.
Magen David Adom assembled and equipped a self-standing field clinic for the disaster zone.

According to ISRAEL21c, Israel also provided aid to several countries with which it has no diplomatic relations, such as Indonesia. The article also listed Sri Lanka among them, but Sri Lanka had already resumed diplomatic relations with Israel in 2000.
According to the Sunday Times of Sri Lanka, the relief operation was initiated by a group of Israelis who had visited Sri Lanka as tourists.
The Israelis who funded the project contacted Gideon Bacharach, manager of the company Hadar Gulf, and said they wanted to assist Sri Lanka.
IsraAID coordinated the efforts of Israeli and Jewish relief organizations, among them Magen David Adom, AJC and B'nai B'rith.
According to ISRAEL21c, the team that left included 14 medical and logistical personnel.
An El Al cargo plane brought a delegation, medical equipment and kitchen equipment to Sri Lanka in the second week of January.
According to Zahavi, the first step was a center for nutritional aid, opened in coordination with the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
According to ISRAEL21c, the team was also to lay the groundwork for future Israeli and Jewish emergency medical and feeding projects.
Zahavi said that feeding people was the top priority for the coming months.
According to him, people needed stations where they could get meals, because they were not in a position to prepare food themselves.
Alongside the clinic, three large kitchens were planned for thousands of people left homeless.
The operation began on January 13 in Balapitiya, with a mobile kitchen, an outdoor medical facility and a trauma-counseling centre.
The kitchen was donated by an Israeli company.
The Ceylon Hotel School Graduates Association and the Chefs Guild of Sri Lanka volunteered to operate the mobile kitchens.
The kitchens served lunch and dinner to nearby camps.
The menu included rice, lentils or potatoes, vegetables, and canned or dried fish.
The meals cost 100,000 rupees a day.
According to the vice president of the graduates association, these camps were the only ones in Sri Lanka to receive a balanced diet made by professional chefs.

stations.title: The Clinic and the Children's Corner

paragraphs.text: The clinic was intended to offer residents medical assistance, with an emphasis on pediatrics and infectious diseases.
At the medical camp in Balapitiya, set up on the initiative of a group of Israelis who had visited Sri Lanka as tourists, Israeli doctors treated about 100 patients every day.
According to the chief doctor of Magen David Adom, most of the patients suffered from wounds, flu, cough and bronchitis.
According to J., at the camp where the Magen David Adom team worked, roaming dogs attacked homeless children, and many of them were bitten.
Israel set up two relief camps in Sri Lanka.
In the second camp, a Magen David Adom team of nine medical professionals treated more than 1,000 patients.
The trauma-counseling centre was decorated with pictures drawn by the children in the camps, and games and activities were held there for the children.
According to J., the team included experts in post-traumatic stress treatment, who also helped children stop bed-wetting.
Israel's Health Minister sent a team of psychologists, at the request of the Sri Lankan ambassador to Israel.
A five-member delegation headed by Dr. Yehuda Baruch of the Abarbanel center was chosen to train local teams over a week.

stations.title: After Half a Year, and After a Year

paragraphs.text: The IsraAID team planned to remain in Sri Lanka as long as finances and the government allowed.
Zahavi said the Israeli teams were among the first to arrive and maintained a continuous presence.
An Israeli-run food center distributed thousands of meals a week, alongside medical aid.
The Israeli team in the Galle region worked with international aid agencies and local groups.

In Southeast Asia, IsraAID also ran programs to strengthen the role of women in supporting their families, to build temporary and permanent housing, and for the psychosocial rehabilitation of the local population.
Zahavi said the locals were thankful, and that everywhere he heard how wonderful the Israelis are.
According to Zahavi, wherever he went, people were always amazed that despite the conflict in the Middle East and all the troubles, the Israelis came to help them.
Prime Minister Ariel Sharon praised the Israeli public's response to the disaster.

On the first anniversary of the tsunami, IsraAID, together with an international group called Project Galle, helped launch in Sri Lanka an exhibition of 1,000 photographs of encounters between volunteers and Sri Lankans displaced by the tsunami.
One source claimed that Israel offered aid out of a belief that it would help warm political relations with India, which rejected outside aid.
Goldman of the Center for Cooperative Studies said that much of the aid creates dependency.
